questions.question: Inside a middleware, what is the difference between calling `next(action)` and `api.dispatch(action)`?
options: There is no difference; both call the reducer directly
`next` passes the action to the next middleware in the chain; `api.dispatch` sends it through the whole chain again from the top
questions.explanation: applyMiddleware gives each middleware a dispatch wrapper that calls the final composed dispatch, so it re-enters the chain from the outermost middleware. next only continues to the following middleware.

questions.question: Why does combineReducers return the previous state object when no slice reducer changed its slice?
options: To save memory on the server
Because reducers are not allowed to create objects
It is required by the Redux DevTools protocol
So reference equality checks in useSelector and memoised selectors can skip work
questions.explanation: Preserving the root reference when nothing changed lets subscribers and selectors detect 'no change' with a cheap === check.

questions.question: Why does the store throw if a reducer calls `dispatch`?
options: The reducer would re-enter the store while the current state is still being computed, breaking the single, predictable state transition
Dispatch is asynchronous and reducers are synchronous
Reducers do not have access to the store
It would bypass the middleware chain, which is forbidden by TypeScript
questions.explanation: The isDispatching guard prevents re-entrant dispatches. Reducers must be pure functions of (state, action) with no side effects.

questions.question: With `applyMiddleware(thunk, logger)`, which middleware sees each action first?
options: logger, because middleware runs right to left
Whichever was registered most recently at runtime
thunk, because compose makes the first middleware the outermost wrapper
questions.explanation: compose(f, g)(x) is f(g(x)), so the first middleware wraps all the others and receives actions first.
